Days ago, OpenAI accused Apple of improperly introducing new evidence in a trade secrets case. Apple struck back today, similarly accusing OpenAI's response of exceeding what court rules permit. Here are the details.

Apple says OpenAI went beyond simply opposing the new evidence

In Apple's lawsuit accusing two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products of misappropriating trade secrets, one of the disputed issues involves a motion for a preliminary injunction.

In short, Apple has asked the court to issue a preliminary injunction, arguing that doing so during the pendency of the case would prevent its trade secrets from being further embedded in OpenAI's hardware development.

As part of the back-and-forth over that motion, Apple filed an opposition brief with five accompanying expert declarations. This immediately drew accusations from the defendants that Apple had improperly introduced new evidence and a request that the court strike portions of the materials.

In their opposition, the defendants (OpenAI and other defendants), in addition to accusing Apple of presenting new evidence, also submitted multiple documents to rebut Apple's arguments.

Apple today filed a reply to the above opposition, accusing the defendants of not simply opposing the new evidence but instead raising new arguments and evidentiary submissions of their own:

Rule 7-3(d)(1) permits a party to oppose new evidence in an opposition brief, but also cautions that the document "must not further argue the motion." The defendants did not honor this limit and instead used their filings to re-litigate the substance of Apple's preliminary injunction motion.

Apple also took issue with a new declaration submitted by Liu, calling it the "most egregious overreach" in the defendants' filings:

Notably, when submitting Liu's declaration, the defendants had argued that the court should only consider that declaration if it simultaneously decided to consider Apple's much-disputed evidence.

That said, Apple contends that, since the defendants have now raised new arguments of their own, the court should consider the entire record rather than striking any evidence from Apple's opposition:

The court has scheduled a hearing on Apple's preliminary injunction motion for October 14.
